issues.legal_issue: A juristic religious endowment cannot be treated as cultivating agricultural land personally merely because the land is worked by servants or hired labour under the management of its human manager.
material_facts: A private religious endowment owned agricultural land and sought possession of land leased to a tenant on the ground that it required the land for personal cultivation.
The endowment was a juristic person, while its manager managed its affairs and any cultivation would be carried out by people acting on its behalf.
The statutory definition allowed certain natural persons with physical or mental disabilities to be deemed to cultivate personally when servants or hired labour cultivated the land.
issues.conclusion: The endowment could not claim that it cultivated the land personally under the disability exception, and was not entitled to possession on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(12) and 2(22) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, personal cultivation requires a direct nexus between the claimant and the agricultural operations through the claimant’s own labour or personal supervision. The disability exception concerns a natural person incapable of personal labour or supervision; it does not extend to a juristic person. The Court relied on Shri Kesheoraj Deo Sansthan, Karanji v. Bapurao Deoba, which explained that personal cultivation requires direct supervision, control, or management and does not permit an intermediary agent between the landlord and the workers.

predicates.personal_cultivation_possession_proceedi: A landlord seeks possession of tenanted agricultural land on the ground that the land is required for personal cultivation.
predicates.claimant_is_juristic_person: The party claiming personal cultivation is a legal entity rather than a natural person.
predicates.cultivation_would_be_by_people_acting_fo: The agricultural work would be done by servants, hired workers, or other people acting on the claimant’s behalf.

issues.definition: When a legal entity seeks possession for personal cultivation and the work would be done by people acting for it, the entity is not treated as cultivating personally.

issues.legal_issue: An entitlement to recover tenanted land for personal cultivation under a repealed enactment does not establish that entitlement under the later governing enactment.
material_facts: The endowment had previously initiated proceedings under an earlier agricultural leases enactment, which had included public charitable trusts among those able to seek possession for personal cultivation.
The possession application at issue was made under a later enactment after the earlier enactment had been repealed.
issues.conclusion: The provisions of the repealed enactment did not assist the endowment in its claim under the later enactment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that provisions of a repealed statute cannot confer an entitlement in proceedings governed by a later enactment. The asserted entitlement had to be established under the law applicable to the possession application.

predicates.tenancy_possession_proceeding_under_late: A party seeks possession of tenanted agricultural land in a proceeding governed by a later enactment.
predicates.claimed_entitlement_depends_on_repealed_: The party relies on an entitlement that appeared in an earlier enactment that has been repealed.

issues.definition: In a possession proceeding governed by later law, reliance on an entitlement found only in repealed law does not supply that entitlement.

issues.legal_issue: A manager of a private religious endowment that is outside the governing public-trust statute cannot claim a trustee’s status under that statute to seek possession for personal cultivation.
material_facts: It was common ground that the religious endowment was a private trust not governed by the Bombay Public Trusts Act.
The endowment’s manager managed its property, but the property was held by the endowment and did not vest in the manager.
The endowment relied on a decision applying the statutory definition of trustee under the public-trust statute.
issues.conclusion: The manager could not qualify as a trustee under that statute, and the cited decision did not assist the endowment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(18) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act defines a trustee to include a manager where the trust property is vested in that person. Ishwardas v. Maharashtra Revenue Tribunal was distinguishable because it concerned a trust governed by that Act and property vested in its trustee or manager. The Court distinguished a trustee from an idol or endowment’s manager or shebait: the former holds trust property, while the latter has possession and management but does not own or hold the property in that capacity.

predicates.tenancy_personal_cultivation_claim: A party seeks possession of tenanted agricultural land for personal cultivation by relying on its manager’s status.
predicates.private_trust_outside_public_trust_law: The trust is private and is not governed by the public-trust law that defines trustees.
predicates.manager_does_not_hold_trust_property: The manager has responsibility for management or possession but the trust property is not vested in the manager as trustee.

issues.definition: When a personal-cultivation claim depends on a manager’s trustee status, that status is unavailable if the private trust is outside the relevant public-trust law and the manager does not hold its property as trustee.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional challenge based on equality or property rights cannot be entertained against a protected land-reform enactment that has received presidential assent.
material_facts: The endowment argued that the provisions preventing it from claiming possession for personal cultivation violated equality and property rights.
The governing enactment had received the President’s assent.
The Court relied on earlier decisions upholding the enactment’s constitutional validity.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional challenge under Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) could not be entertained because Article 31A rendered the enactment immune from that challenge.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A of the Constitution protects qualifying land-reform legislation from challenge under Articles 14 and 19. The Court relied on Shri Mahadeo Paikaji Kolhe Yavatmal v. The State of Bombay and Sri Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. The State of Bombay, which upheld the relevant legislation against constitutional challenge.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A party challenges legislation governing agricultural land or tenancy as unconstitutional.
predicates.law_received_presidential_assent: The challenged land-reform law received the President’s assent.
predicates.challenge_invokes_equality_or_property_r: The constitutional challenge relies on equality or property-right protections.

issues.definition: A challenge to land-reform legislation based on equality or property rights is barred when the law received presidential assent and the constitutional land-reform immunity applies.
